Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.51 8.3 Orbits and stabilisers Definition 8.3.1. Let X be a G-set. The orbit of x ∈ X is Gx = {λ(g)x ∶ g ∈ G}. It is the set of all images of x under the action of G. In the special case that Gx = X, we say that the action is transitive. Definition 8.3.2. Fix x ∈ X. The stabiliser of x is denoted by StabG(x), and is defined to be StabG(x) = {g ∈ G ∶ λ(g)x = x}. Example 8.3.3. G = S4 and X = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Note X is a G-set via the action λ(g)i = gi. • Orbits: G1 = {1, 2, 3, 4} = G2 = G3 = G4. This action is transitive. • Stabilisers: StabG(1) = {all things in S4 that fix 1} = {e, (2 3 4), (2 4 3), (2 3), (2 4), (3 4)} StabG(2) = {all things in S4 that fix 2} = {e, (1 3 4), (1 4 3), (1 3), (1 4), (3 4)} Etc. In all cases note that StabG(i) ≅ S3. Example 8.3.4. (Easy example). Recall from Example 8.1.9 that there is a natural action of D8 = {e, ρ, ρ 2, ρ 3, σ, σρ, σρ 2, σρ3} (where ρ = (1 2 3 4) and σ = (1 4)(2 3)) on the cube C below, via: λ(ρ) = (1 2 3 4)(5 6 7 8) and λ(σ) = (1 4)(2 3)(5 8)(6 7) and λ(σiρj) = λ(σ)iλ(ρ)j. 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 • Orbits: The orbit of corner 1 is {1, 2, 3, 4} (this is also the orbit of corner 2, corner 3 and corner 4) and the orbit of corner 5 is {5, 6, 7, 8}. The action is not transitive. • Stabilisers: For corner 1 we have that StabD8 (1) = {e, (2 4)(6 8)} = {e, σρ 3}. The stabilisers of other corners can be worked out similarly. Example 8.3.5. Recall from Example 8.1.7 that any group G acts on itself (i.e. X = G) via the regular action: λ(g)x = gx for all g ∈ G and all x ∈ X = G. • Orbits: The orbit of e ∈ X is Ge = {ge ∶ g ∈ G} = G = X. The action is transitive. [Exercise: show that the orbit of any x ∈ X is also equal to X.] • Stabilisers: For any x ∈ X = G notice that gx = x ⟺ g = e. Therefore we have that StabG(x) = {g ∈ G ∶ λ(g)x = x} = ⟨e⟩. Example 8.3.6. Recall from Example 8.1.8 that any group G acts on itself (i.e. X = G) via the conjugation action: λ(g)x = gxg−1 for all g ∈ G and all x ∈ X = G. • Orbits: The orbit of e ∈ X is Ge = {geg−1 ∶ g ∈ G} = {e}. The action is not transitive when G /= ⟨e⟩. Working out Gx = {gxg−1 ∶ g ∈ G} for other elements x ∈ G depends on the group G. [Exercise: if G is abelian show that the orbit of any x ∈ X is equal to {x}.] • Stabilisers: For any x ∈ X = G, by definition StabG(x) = {g ∈ G ∶ gxg−1 = x} = {g ∈ G ∶ g−1xg = x}. This set plays a special role in group theory and is called the centraliser of x in G.

# Page 2^page=2
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.52 8.3.1 Handout for Section 8.3 Example 8.3.7. H = {e, (12)(34)} and X = {{1, 2}, {1, 3}, {1, 4}, {2, 3}, {2, 4}, {3, 4}}. Note X is an H-set via the action λ(h){i, j} = {hi, hj}. • Orbits: H{1, 2} = {{1, 2}} H{1, 3} = {{1, 3}, {2, 4}} H{1, 4} = {{1, 4}, {2, 3}} H{2, 3} = {{2, 3}, {1, 4}} H{2, 4} = {{2, 4}, {1, 3}} H{3,4} = {{3,4}} Notice that H{1, 3} = H{2, 4} and H{1, 4} = H{2, 3}. This action is not transitive. • Stabilisers: StabH ({1, 2}) = {all things in H that either fix 1 and 2 or interchange 1 and 2} So StabH ({1, 2}) = {e, (1 2)(3 4)} and similarly StabH ({3, 4}) = {e, (1 2)(3 4)}. On the other hand, StabH ({1, 3}) = {e}, StabH ({2, 4}) = {e}, StabH ({1, 4}) = {e}, StabH ({2, 3}) = {e} Question 8.3.8. Let K = {e, (123), (132)} and X = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Note X is a K-set via the action λ(g)i = gi. Find the orbits of K on X and the stabilisers of all things in X. Is the action transitive? • Orbits: K1 = {1, 2, 3} = K2 = K3 and K4 = {4}. The action is not transitive. • Stabilisers: StabK (1) = StabK (2) = StabK (3) = e and StabK (4) = K.

# Page 3^page=3
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.55 9 The orbit stabiliser theorem and the orbit count- ing theorem 9.1 The orbit stabiliser theorem Here we note some facts that you will prove on problems sheets. Proposition 9.1.0. Let X be a G-set and x, y ∈ X. (i) Either Gx = Gy or Gx ∩ Gy = ∅. In other words, orbits are disjoint or they are equal. (The above result means that every G-set can be partitioned into a union of disjoint orbits X = Orb1 ∪ Orb2 ∪ . . . ∪ Orbn.) (ii) If x and y lie in the same orbit, then Gx = Gy. (iii) If Y is an orbit and x ∈ Y , then Gx = Y . (iv) StabG(x) is a subgroup of G. If you find a partition of X into orbits Orb1 ∪ . . . ∪ Orbn and we choose an element xi ∈ Orbi from each orbit, then {x1, . . . , xn} is called a set of orbit representatives of the G-set X. We now give the Orbit Stabiliser Theorem. This powerful result allows us to calculate the size of any orbit once we know the size of the appropriate stabiliser. We can use this to answer questions like: “Can D10 act transitively on the corners of a triangle?” Theorem 9.1.1. (Orbit Stabiliser Theorem.) Let G be a group, and let X be a G-set. For all x ∈ X the size of the orbit Gx is given by the formula, ∣Gx∣ = [G ∶ StabG(x)]. In particular, if G is finite then we have ∣Gx∣ = ∣G∣/∣StabG(x)∣. Proof. To simplify our notation, we define S = StabG(x). Let λ be the action of G on X. Fix g, h ∈ G and note that λ(g)x, λ(h)x ∈ Gx. Now λ(g)x /= λ(h)x ⟺ λ(h −1)λ(g)x /= λ(h−1)λ(h)x ⟺ λ(h −1g)x /= λ(h−1h)x ⟺ λ(h −1g)x /= x ⟺ h −1g /∈ S ⟺ gS /= hS (by Theorem 4.1.3) Since λ(g)x /= λ(h)x ⟺ gS /= hS, the number of distinct elements in the orbit Gx is equal to the number of distinct cosets of S in G, which we recall is denoted by [G ∶ StabG(x)]. This proves the main part of the theorem. Finally, we notice that if G is finite, then by Lagrange’s Theorem we have [G ∶ StabG(x)] = ∣G∣/∣StabG(x)∣. Example 9.1.2. Recall that in Example 8.3.3 we had G = S4 and X = {1, 2, 3, 4}, with X a G-set via the action λ(g)i = gi. In that example we saw that G1 = {1, 2, 3, 4} so ∣G1∣ = 4. We also saw that StabG(1) = {e, (2 3 4), (2 4 3), (2 3), (2 4), (3 4)}, so ∣StabG(1)∣ = 6. The Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem tells us that ∣G1∣ = ∣G∣/∣StabG(1)∣, which is true in this case, since 4 = 4!/6. Example 9.1.3. Let G be a group of order 20. We can prove, using the Orbit Stabiliser Theorem, that there is no transitive action of G on a set of size 6. First, let’s recall the definition of a transitive action. An action λ of G on a set X is transitive if there is some x ∈ X such that the orbit Gx is all of X. Suppose X has size 6 and such a transitive action λ exists. Then there is some x ∈ X such that Gx = X. Hence ∣Gx∣ = 6. Using the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem, we have 6 = ∣Gx∣ = ∣G∣/∣StabG(x)∣ = 20/∣StabG(x)∣. Since ∣StabG(x)∣ is an integer, this is impossible. Hence there is no orbit of G of size 6.

Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.56 9.1.1 Handout for Section 9.1 Question 9.1.4. Can D10 act transitively on the corners of a triange? Solution: No! Suppose the answer is yes. Then D10 has a transitive action on a set X of size 3. Hence there is some x ∈ X such that ∣D10x∣ = 3. By the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem we have 3 = ∣D10x∣ = ∣D10∣/∣StabD10 (x)∣ = 10/∣StabD10 (x)∣, which is impossible because ∣StabD10 (x)∣ is an integer. Example 9.1.5. Let G = Sn and let Y = {1, 2, . . . , n}. There is a natural action of G on the set Y × Y via the action, λ(g)(x, y) = (gx, gy). So for example λ((1 2 3))(1, 3) = ((1 2 3)1, (1 2 3)3) = (2, 3) and λ((1 2))(2, 3) = ((1 2)2, (1 2)3) = (1, 3). What is the size of the orbit G(1, 1)? We could calculate this directly, or we could use the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem. To use the theorem, we need to know ∣G∣ = n! and ∣StabG((1, 1))∣. Now StabG((1, 1)) = {all things in Sn that fix 1} = Sym({2, 3, . . . , n}). We know that Sym({2, 3, . . . , n}), being the group of all permutations of n − 1 things, has size (n − 1)!. Hence ∣StabG((1, 1))∣ = (n − 1)!. Now we can use the Orbit Stabiliser Theorem to calculate that ∣G(1, 1)∣ = ∣G∣/∣StabG((1, 1))∣ = n!/(n − 1)! = n.
